Rome has been lived in for nearly 3,000 years and almost nothing was thrown away. Temples became churches, churches were buried under newer churches, and the ground rose by metres. That is why this map goes down as often as it goes out.

## Layers

**Ancient (to about 500).** The Forum, the Capitol and the Tiber island are the old core; the Aurelian Wall still rings the centre. Under many churches you can stand in Roman houses and temples.

**Papal Rome (500–1870).** For 1,300 years the city was ruled by the popes. They built the churches, the confraternities that buried the dead and comforted the condemned, the hospitals and the flood plaques; they also ran the executions.

**Capital of Italy (1870–1922).** Italian troops broke through at Porta Pia in 1870. The new state built Prati and the Esquilino, Protestant and Jewish buildings appeared inside the walls, and the river was walled in after the flood of 1870.

**Fascism and war (1922–1945).** Mussolini cut avenues through the old city, moved the poor to borgate on the edge, and planned EUR for a world's fair that never opened. In 1943–44 Rome was bombed and occupied; the marks are small but exact.

**The Republic (1946–).** The city spread over the Campagna in housing estates: INA-Casa villages, then megastructures like Corviale and Laurentino. The Church raced to give each new estate a parish, and those churches are the best modern buildings on the map.

## Bearings

The Tiber curves through from north to south-west. The centre is the bend (Campo Marzio, Navona, Pantheon); the Vatican and Prati are across the river to the west; Trastevere and the Gianicolo to the south-west; the Esquilino and San Lorenzo east of Termini. Metro A runs north-west to south-east, B north-east to south through EUR, C east.

## What this map is for

The main thing is the church hunt: the strangest religious building of each period, and a full day for modern ones. Around it are concrete, abandoned places, small marks with real stories, and a minor layer of film and book locations. Start with "Church day" under Routes › Tours by topic.

Rome has more than 900 churches, and the interesting ones are rarely the famous ones.

**The ancient trick: reuse.** Santa Maria Antiqua is an imperial hall painted for three centuries; San Nicola in Carcere swallowed three temples; Santi Cosma e Damiano is a library with a round temple for a porch; Santa Maria degli Angeli is a bath house. Go underneath at San Clemente, the Case Romane or Santa Passera and you walk through every layer.

**The Baroque trick: illusion.** Borromini made walls move at Sant'Ivo; Pozzo painted a dome on a flat canvas at Sant'Ignazio. These are experiments in geometry and perspective, and they are meant to be stood in at the right spot.

**The macabre and the scientific.** Confraternities buried the drowned and kept their skulls (Orazione e Morte); friars made chandeliers of bones; a meridian in a church tested the calendar; a column on the Capitol was drilled, perhaps to sight the sun.

**The modern race.** After 1945 Rome grew by a million people in estates with no churches. The Vicariate built hundreds of parishes, and the best of them are startling: Busiri Vici's raw concrete at Casal Bruciato, Nervi's pyramid at San Gaspare, Spadolini and Morandi's sunlight cross at Tor Bella Monaca, Meier's sails for the year 2000. Add the Waldensian concrete church, the Great Synagogue, Portoghesi's mosque and a Chinese pagoda behind warehouse walls, and you have a day.

Start with: Church day: modern religious buildings (Tours by topic), or the all-eras version if you want the whole story in one day.

Rome's modern architecture is mostly on the edge, and much of it is half-finished, closed or rotting, which is why it is so interesting.

**Estates.** The Fascist borgate (Quarticciolo, the Trullo) were where the regime put the poor it evicted from the centre. After the war INA-Casa built humane villages (Tuscolano, with Libera's walled kasbah). In the 1970s–80s came the megastructures: Corviale, a single block almost a kilometre long, and Laurentino 38 with its bridge-buildings over a ring road.

**Events.** EUR was built for a world's fair that never opened. The 1960 Olympics left Nervi's stadium (closed since 2011), his Palazzetto and viaduct, and a velodrome that was blown up in 2008. Calatrava's swimming sail stood unfinished for fifteen years.

**Abandoned institutions.** The Forlanini sanatorium, the asylum of Santa Maria della Pietà, the Penicillina factory that Fleming opened in 1950, the soap works of Mira Lanza: most are closed or dangerous, so look from outside.

Start with: Corviale, Tor di Valle and the Penicillina, while they still exist.

Some of the best things in Rome take thirty seconds to see.

**Floods.** More than a hundred plaques show how high the Tiber rose; the oldest still in the street is from 1277, under the Arco dei Banchi. The Ripetta gauge is still the city's zero.

**1849.** French cannonballs from the siege of the Roman Republic are still in a church wall, on an altar and on the stairs of a palace.

**Edicts.** About 67 papal marble plaques of 1646–1790 forbid dumping rubbish, one in Via Margutta with lashes, the stocks and the wheel; another forbids people, by mistake, *not* to dump it.

**1944 and after.** Via Rasella's bullet holes, the Ghetto's brass stones, the plaques for Teresa Gullace and Giorgiana Masi, and the spot where Moro's body was found.

Start with: Arco dei Banchi, Via Margutta, Via Rasella.

Neorealist directors filmed on real streets just after the war, so Pigneto and Via Francesco Crispi look much as they did in *Roma città aperta* and *Ladri di biciclette*. Fellini rebuilt Via Veneto at Cinecittà. Hollywood built St Peter's Square in California for *Angels & Demons* and the Spanish Steps in England for *Mission: Impossible*. *Spectre* turned a Fascist museum into a cemetery.

For books, Goethe's flat on the Corso, Hawthorne's tower of Hilda, Henry James's Protestant Cemetery, Gadda's Via Merulana and Morante's bombed San Lorenzo are all on the map.

Start with: the Rome on screen tour.

- **Churches close at midday**, usually about 12:00–16:00/16:30. San Gaspare del Bufalo, the Jubilee Church and Hua Yi Si stay open, so plan them for lunchtime.
- **Book ahead:** Santa Maria Antiqua (Forum SUPER/Full Experience ticket), San Clemente underground (timed), Santi Marcellino e Pietro catacomb, Santo Spirito in Sassia (email), Villa Torlonia bunker, the Soratte bunker.
- **Narrow windows:** Sant'Ivo Mon–Fri 9:30–13:30; the Mosque Wed and Sat mornings; the Ossario Garibaldino Thursday morning; Galleria Colonna Fri–Sat mornings; Santa Passera Sunday Mass; the Russian church weekends; the Synagogue not on Saturday.
- **Once a year:** Sacconi Rossi crypt (2 Nov), San Giovanni Decollato (24 June).
- **Free:** Fosse Ardeatine, Via Tasso, Santa Costanza, most churches. The Non-Catholic Cemetery expects a cash donation.
- **Dress:** shoulders and knees covered in churches; at the Mosque women cover their heads and everyone removes shoes.
- **Getting out:** Metro B for EUR and Laurentino; Metro C for Tor Bella Monaca; the Roma–Lido train for Vitinia and Ostia; the Roma–Viterbo train for the Mosque. A car day helps for Malafede, Prima Porta and Settebagni.
- Prices and hours change; check on the day.

Drafted 6 Nov 2026 from the site list (ids in brackets). Undecided between a modern-religious-buildings day and an all-eras hunt; Kon leans to modern. Hours are indicative (Google Places, Nov 2026, plus sources in the register): most Catholic churches close ~12:00–16:30, so every option puts the all-day-open stops at midday.

**Recommendation:** Option A. The modern day is the one that needs a plan (the buildings are spread over the periphery, and no guide strings them together). The ancient-to-Baroque oddities are dense in the centre, so they can sit as stops on the ordinary area walks. Option B is the fallback if he wants the "whole story in one day" feeling.

## Option A — Modern religious buildings, 1897–2013 (one day, metro + train + bus)
Order follows the city more than the calendar; the clue to find at each stop is in brackets.
1. **Tempio Valdese** — 1911–14, Rome's first reinforced-concrete church. Exterior any time (the "LUX LUCET IN TENEBRIS" lunette); inside only Tue 17–19 / Sat 11–13 or by asking.
2. **San Gioacchino** — 1897 aluminium dome pierced with crystal stars. 7 min walk. Open from 6:30.
3. **Sacro Cuore di Cristo Re** — Piacentini, 1920–34. 10 min walk. Optional.
4. **Sacro Cuore Immacolato di Maria** — the dome that was never built; find its plaster model in the right-hand pier. Tram/bus to Piazza Euclide.
5. **Great Mosque** — only Wed/Sat mornings; one stop on the Roma–Viterbo train from Piazza Euclide to Acqua Acetosa. On other days: **San Valentino + Corso Francia viaduct** instead.
6. *Midday, all-day-open stops:* **San Gaspare del Bufalo** — Nervi's last church, entered at a corner (Metro A Arco di Travertino; open 7:30–21) → **Dio Padre Misericordioso** — Meier (Metro C Torre Maura + bus 556; 7:30–19) → **Hua Yi Si** — pagoda behind warehouse walls (10:30–15; shoes off).
7. **Santa Maria Madre del Redentore** — Spadolini + Morandi, the cross made of sunlight between two pinnacles; with the Tor Bella Monaca towers.
8. *If time is left (from 16:30):* **Santa Maria della Visitazione** — Busiri Vici's raw concrete — and **San Vincenzo Pallotti**, 900 m apart. These are the most brutalist pair in Rome; swap them in for 2–3 if they matter more than the Prati trio.

Day: Wednesday or Saturday (Mosque); not Monday (Cafasso closed, if added). Expect 7–9 stops.

**A2 — second modern day, south-west (optional):** La Salette → Gesù Divin Lavoratore → Santo Volto di Gesù + Santa Passera opposite (2006 vs a 2nd-c. tomb under a medieval church) → Santi Pietro e Paolo, EUR + Velodromo crater → Roma–Lido train to Vitinia → San Pio da Pietrelcina, Malafede.

## Option B — All eras, one day ("the whole story")
Only on Mon, Tue, Thu or Fri (Sant'Ivo is weekday mornings; San Nicola closes Wed; the Synagogue is shut Sat).
1. 9:30 **Santa Maria Antiqua** — 6th c. (Forum SUPER ticket, book).
2. **San Nicola in Carcere** — walk between three Republican temples under the church.
3. **San Bartolomeo all'Isola** — 998, on the Asclepius site; the 1849 cannonball.
4. **Aracoeli drilled column** — medieval; the "meridian" that probably wasn't.
5. by 13:00 **Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza** — Borromini's star and spiral (Mon–Fri 9:30–13:30); **Sant'Ignazio** next door if open — the flat dome.
6. 14:00 **Great Synagogue** — 1904 square aluminium dome (museum tour).
7. Metro east: **San Gaspare del Bufalo** — 1981.
8. **Dio Padre Misericordioso** — 2003.
Swap-ins: Santo Stefano Rotondo or San Clemente for 2–3 (closed Mon); Orazione e Morte (check restoration) for 4.

## Option C — Two days
Day 1 = Option B steps 1–6 (centre, ancient → 1904). Day 2 = Option A. Least rushing; the full arc is kept.

## Not in any option (and why)
Sacconi Rossi (2 Nov only), San Giovanni Decollato (24 Jun only), Dino Compagni and Commodilla (permit), Sabaudia, Subiaco, San Nilo (day trips), Santo Stefano degli Abissini (no access).

## Verdicts and corrections

### Religious buildings
- **Santa Maria della Presentazione** — C2 was wrong. The church is at **Via di Torrevecchia 1104** (Primavalle), by **Glauco and Roberto Gresleri, 1997–2000**: a concrete cylinder entered below street level, a hanging "stalactite" cross of two blades, roof garden. Nemesi designed only the separate civic-religious centre in Quartaccio (2002). Pin 41.91206, 12.40105. Pope Leo XIV visited 8 Mar 2026. Sources: Turismo Roma; Vatican News, Mar 2026; GRAS 2008 leaflet.
- **Santa Maria della Visitazione** — confirmed at **Via dei Crispolti 142**, Collatino/Casal Bruciato; Busiri Vici 1965–71 (Domus says 1969–71; Turismo Roma 1965–71), consecrated 22 Oct 1971. Open winter 7:30–12:00 and 16:30–19:00; Jun–Aug 17:00–19:00 only. Domus: concave front, convex back, ribbon windows, concrete-and-river-gravel floor. Pin 41.90988, 12.55129.
- **San Vincenzo Pallotti** (hypar vault, C2 lead) — address found: **Via Matteo Tondi 80**, Pietralata area; consecrated 1996. Pin 41.91807, 12.55661 (Turismo Roma). It is 900 m from the Visitazione: pair them.
- **Santo Volto di Gesù** (Magliana, Via della Magliana 162) — architects are **Piero Sartogo and Nathalie Grenon** (2003–06); inside, Mimmo Paladino's Via Crucis and a Carla Accardi window. Across the road from Santa Passera (C1): an ancient–modern pair.
- **Gesù Divin Lavoratore** (Via Oderisi da Gubbio 16, Portuense) — added. Raffaello Fagnoni 1955–60: oval hall on 14 stone-clad concrete piers, ribbed concrete ceiling, cylindrical bell tower that doubles as the entrance portal (BeWeB; Domus "5 chiese del Novecento"). Pin 41.86854, 12.46650.
- **Sacro Cuore di Gesù Agonizzante, Vitinia** — added as a strong lead: Ildo Avetta, 1955; called "one of the best churches in Rome of the period" by the Churches of Rome Wiki author. Pin 41.79107, 12.40691. Pairs with San Pio (Malafede) and San Pier Damiani (Acilia).
- **Preziosissimo Sangue, Tor di Quinto** — the building is the parish hall; the proper church was never built (Churches of Rome Wiki review). An "unfinished church" story, not a brutalist highlight. Pin 41.94615, 12.47400.
- **Santi Sette Fondatori** (Piazza Salerno 4) — round church, Alberto Tonelli 1946–56; marble lower drum. Pin 41.91081, 12.51295.
- **SS. Corpo e Sangue di Cristo** (Via Narni 19) and **Santa Gemma Galgani** (Via Monte Meta 1) — both Aldo Aloysi (with Vichi), 1988–91, exposed concrete; reviewers call them plain boxes. Keep as extras.
- **Santa Francesca Romana all'Ardeatino** — date conflict: D1 (BeWeB) 1967–69 vs the Churches of Rome Wiki author "1938, Giuseppe Zander". Unresolved; extra only.
- **San Romano Martire** (Largo Beltramelli 23, Pietralata) — 2002–04, Igino Pineschi, Rupnik/Centro Aletti apse mosaic. Not the "ribcage pagoda" church of C2. **That lead stays unresolved** (vediromainbici 2022-05-29 page not found by search); drop until someone finds the name.
- **Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza** — confirmed reopened 27 Oct 2026, **Mon–Fri 9:30–13:30, free**, TCI volunteers (Finestre sull'Arte, 27 Oct 2026; SiViaggia).
- **Santa Maria dell'Orazione e Morte** — status uncertain: Fanpage says not visitable, closed for works; Soprintendenza has a PNRR restoration project for the interior decoration (Mar 2026); crypt hours in C1 conflict. Treat as "check before going".
- **Santa Rita da Cascia in Campitelli** — deconsecrated; now **Sala Santa Rita**, a city exhibition space (Via Montanara), open Tue–Sat 17–19 during shows. Moved stone by stone in 1928.
